content: Antibiotics have been explored as a potential treatment for ulcerative colitis (UC) due to their ability to target intestinal bacteria associated with inflammation. However, concerns remain regarding their effectiveness and safety in this context. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether antibiotic therapy is both safe and effective for inducing and maintaining remission in individuals with UC. A systematic search of five electronic databases was conducted on December 10, 2021, to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared antibiotic therapy to either placebo or an active comparator. The inclusion criteria allowed for participants of all ages with UC who were treated with antibiotics of any type, dose, or route of administration. For induction studies, a minimum treatment duration of two weeks was required, while maintenance studies required a minimum duration of three months. The analysis included 12 RCTs involving a total of 847 participants. Among these, one study focused on maintenance of remission using antibiotics alone compared to 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA). The remaining trials investigated antibiotics as an adjunct therapy alongside standard care regimens or other medications, or compared antibiotics to other adjunct therapies for their role in inducing remission. High-certainty evidence demonstrated that antibiotics, when compared to placebo, did not result in a significant difference in the failure to achieve clinical remission (risk ratio [RR] 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.74 to 1.06). Subgroup analyses revealed no differences when additional therapies such as steroids, steroids plus 5-ASA, or steroids plus 5-ASA plus probiotics were used alongside antibiotics or placebo. Low-certainty evidence suggested that antibiotics, compared to placebo, may not significantly differ in terms of failure to achieve a clinical response (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.22). Similarly, subgroup analyses showed no differences when steroids or steroids plus 5-ASA were used as additional therapies. Regarding safety, low-certainty evidence indicated that antibiotics, compared to placebo, may not significantly differ in the occurrence of serious adverse events (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.38 to 3.71) or withdrawals due to adverse events (RR 2.06, 95% CI 0.27 to 15.72). Subgroup analyses again found no differences when steroids or steroids plus 5-ASA were used as additional therapies. The evidence was very uncertain regarding the effects of antibiotics combined with probiotics compared to no treatment or placebo for failure to achieve clinical remission (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.19), serious adverse events (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 15.08), or withdrawals due to adverse events (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 15.08). Similarly, very low-certainty evidence made it unclear whether antibiotics differed from 5-ASA in failure to achieve clinical remission (RR 2.20, 95% CI 1.17 to 4.14) or from probiotics in failure to achieve clinical remission (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.94). The evidence was also very uncertain regarding the comparison of antibiotics to 5-ASA for failure to maintain clinical remission (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.06) or to no treatment for failure to achieve clinical remission in a mixed population of active and inactive disease (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.07). For other outcomes, the lack of sufficient data precluded any meaningful conclusions. In conclusion, high-certainty evidence indicates no difference between antibiotics and placebo in the proportion of individuals achieving clinical remission at the end of the intervention period. However, there is some evidence suggesting that antibiotics may lead to a higher proportion of individuals achieving clinical remission and possibly clinical response compared to placebo at 12 months. There appears to be no significant difference in the occurrence of serious adverse events or withdrawals due to adverse events between antibiotics and placebo. Further research is needed, particularly focusing on comparisons of antibiotics and placebo in conjunction with standard therapies, with longer-term outcome measurements. Additionally, future studies could explore head-to-head comparisons of antibiotics with other treatments, as current evidence in this area is limited to single studies.
